meta.regime: Two of yesterday's three legs reversed inside a day: the Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% against pricing near 90% for a hike and took NZD/USD down 1.31%, while an Iranian claim that a tanker struck naval mines east of Hormuz put the crude premium straight back on, WTI at 101.423 and up 4.40% on the week, which dragged the US ten-year back above 5% to 5.0250 and ended yesterday's one-day duration rally. What survives is the French repair, with the OAT-Bund spread holding near 157 basis points, and the franc at the bottom of the board - except that the kiwi is now down there beside it, which is the single biggest change to the trade list.
meta.nextBigEvent: The FOMC at 18:00 UTC with Chair Warsh's press conference at 18:30, where a hold is 90-94% priced and December near 80%, so there is nothing hawkish left to buy and considerable room to disappoint - preceded by Healey's first UK Budget at 12:30 and the Bank of Canada with a Monetary Policy Report at 13:45, then US advance Q3 GDP and September core PCE at 12:30 Thursday with the ECB at 13:15, and the Bank of Japan Outlook Report at 02:31 UTC Friday.

dailyRead: The thing that changed overnight was a central bank refusing to do what the market had already paid for, and it is worth being precise about the size of the surprise. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held the Official Cash Rate at 2.75% on a 4-3 vote - Breman, Carl Hansen, Prasanna Gai and Rebecca Williams to hold, Paul Conway, Hayley Gourley and Karen Silk for 25 basis points - against pricing that sources put between 90% and 100% for a hike to 3.00%. NZD/USD fell close to a cent in minutes and TradingEconomics now carries it at 0.56073, down 1.31% on the day, 1.63% on the week and 2.58% year to date; the New Zealand ten-year fell about 3.5 basis points to 4.9450. This file owes a correction on what happened next, because it got the three hours after the press conference wrong. At 02:00 UTC the hawkish branch landed - Breman said further increases are likely at coming meetings, that policy could move into restrictive territory, and that the Committee is concerned a sustained weak kiwi adds to imported inflation - and this file read that as a floor under the currency, arguing that a Governor who names the exchange rate as an inflation channel makes further weakness self-limiting. The price has since gone lower, not higher. That specific leg broke: conditional guidance from a Committee that has just declined a 90%-priced hike is not worth a floor, and the honest conclusion is that the kiwi is a sell until the data Breman named actually arrives. New Zealand goes from zero to minus 1 and from MIXED to WEAKENING. The second reversal is the oil premium, and it reversed on a dated incident rather than on sentiment. Iran's navy said on Tuesday October 27 that an oil tanker caught fire after striking naval mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, that the vessel had switched off its tracking and entered a restricted zone, and that the strait remains unsafe and closed to ships attempting to pass without coordination; there is no independent confirmation of the Iranian account, exactly as there was none for the October 17 claim. WTI is 101.423 and up 1.52%, now 4.40% higher on the week, 13.47% on the month and 76.63% year to date; Brent is 115.502 and up 1.42%, 6.14% on the week, with the Brent-WTI spread widening to 14.08 dollars. Reuters, on Kpler data, counts at least eighteen tanker attacks in the last two weeks, and the United States is urging shippers onto a southern route through the strait that Tehran regards as illegal. Say plainly what this does to yesterday's call. This file spent two days building the case that the premium was deflating because barrels were rerouting - strait flows back near 82% of pre-war levels, total Middle East flows above 24 million barrels a day against 23.3 million before the war, 40% of non-Iranian Gulf crude moving by pipeline against 17% - and that evidence is not wrong. What was wrong was the inference. The premium is not priced off volumes alone, it is priced off insurable risk, and a mine field reprices insurance regardless of how many barrels get through. Rerouting caps the upside; it does not deflate the premium while the mines are still being laid. USOIL goes from RANGE to a MEDIUM long on that, and it is the first time in a week this file has been long the barrel. The third reversal is duration, and it is the one that should make anyone cautious about yesterday's framing. Yesterday every ten-year on this board fell together with equities rising, and this file called that an inflation premium coming out rather than a growth scare. It lasted one session. The US ten-year is back above 5% at 5.0250, the JGB rose to 2.8310, the Australian ten-year to 5.2200, the OAT to 4.9220 and the BTP to 4.5100; only New Zealand, on its own dovish surprise, and Switzerland at 0.4570 fell. Equities have held their bid - the S&P near 7,723 and up 0.60%, the Nasdaq Composite 26,478 and up 1.18%, the Nikkei 63,268 and up 1.73%, the VIX down to 17.52 - so the configuration is now equities up and yields up, which is the signature of an inflation premium going back in rather than coming out. That matters for the Fed in thirteen hours more than anything else in this file. Australia keeps the top of the board and the reason is that the one number this file flagged as unverifiable yesterday has now printed, in the hawkish direction. TradingEconomics carries the Trimmed Mean CPI QoQ at 1.0% against 0.8% previously, which is exactly the Reserve Bank's own August forecast of 0.8% beaten by two tenths and exactly what Deputy Governor Hauser pre-flagged in public; the annual trimmed mean is 3.7% against a 3.6% consensus, headline CPI 4.3% y/y against 4.2% and 0.8% m/m against 0.7%, and quarterly headline 1.3% q/q. ANZ says the data cements the case for a November hike and CBA has moved its forecast to a hike. But be honest about what that does to the trade rather than to the thesis: November 3 pricing has gone from the 50-60% this file was buying to somewhere between 78% on FXStreet's read and near 90% on the ABC's, and AUD/USD responded with plus 0.12% on the day and plus 0.06% on the week. The asymmetry has been spent. Australia stays at plus 3 because the data case is genuinely the strongest here - the highest policy rate on the board at 4.60%, accelerating inflation, a core measure beating the Bank's own forecast, and a ten-year 476 basis points above the franc - but the forward goes from an unpriced hawkish decision to a priced one, and that changes where you express it. Own the Aussie against the kiwi and the franc, not against the dollar. The counterweight is unchanged and still real: a services PMI of 47.8 and manufacturing at 49.7, five-year-high 4.7% unemployment and September employment down 39,329. Canada improves and both of yesterday's reasons for cutting it are now half-repaired. The barrel is the first and most direct: at 101.423 and plus 4.40% on the week, the terms-of-trade leg this file removed yesterday is back, and the Brent-WTI spread at 14.08 dollars still means Canadian crude captures less of the move than Brent headlines imply. The second is the policy signal. Macklem told reporters on Saturday that the Bank's quarterly inflation forecasts are likely to be revised higher, which markets read as a hint, and interest-rate futures moved from roughly 30% for an October hike to about three in four. The forecaster split that worried this file yesterday has not closed - a Reuters poll of 34 economists taken October 21-23 has 56% expecting 25 basis points to 2.50%, against pricing near 75-80% - so the gap is still about twenty points and a hold would be a sharp move the other way. Canada stays at plus 1 rather than going to plus 2, because a binary with a 44% minority against it eight and a half hours away does not deserve an upgrade in advance; what it deserves is a better forward, and it gets one. The yen is the currency this file is marking down, and the reason is the leg that broke rather than the policy case. Yesterday's read said explicitly that a deflating crude premium gives something to the yen as the most energy-import-levered economy on this board. Crude stopped deflating today, and the transmission is immediate: USD/JPY is 157.807 and has sat near 158 through the Asian session, the JGB rose to 2.8310 but the US ten-year rose further to 5.0250 so the disadvantage widened to about 219 basis points, and reporting attributes the yen's inability to hold its gains directly to higher import costs. The policy case is untouched and still good - a Bloomberg survey has 83% of economists expecting a December hike against 35% a month ago, MUFG expects Friday's Outlook Report to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached 2%, Reuters frames it as the Bank declaring victory in a nearly fourteen-year battle, and Daiwa expects the FY26 growth forecast lifted to 0.8% from 0.6% and FY27 core CPI to 2.5% from 2.4% - but Bloomberg also reports officials seeing little need for consecutive hikes absent a sudden rise in upside inflation risk, and the two-way vote risk stands, with Takata possibly proposing a hike again and the two September dissenters able to call for a cut. Japan goes to zero and MIXED, and the consequence runs through the crosses: USD/JPY and EUR/JPY both come off their shorts to RANGE, CHF/JPY loses its HIGH, and the JPY basket goes to RANGE by its own rule. Sterling holds plus 1 into the single most dangerous hour of its week. The data is still the best cyclical set here - CPI 3.5% with core 2.8%, an October composite PMI of 53.1, unemployment down to 4.7%, employment plus 102,000 - and November 5 is 94-97% priced for 4.00%. The Budget lands at 12:30 UTC and one detail has changed in the reporting: this is Chancellor John Healey's first Budget, and an FP Markets preview frames the pound's reaction as conditional on why gilt yields move, with a growth-driven rise sterling-positive and a risk-driven rise sterling-negative. TradingEconomics describes gilt markets as unusually calm going in despite ambitious spending plans not yet fully costed, which is a setup where the asymmetry is to the downside. With the ten-year gilt at 5.3529 and still the highest yield on this board, GBP/USD comes off its long to RANGE: a Budget at 12:30 and an FOMC at 18:30 on opposite legs of the same pair on the same day is not a 4H swing, it is a coin flip with two faces. The dollar stays at zero and the press conference stays the biggest single asymmetry in this file. A Reuters poll has 94 of 100 economists expecting the hold and CME FedWatch implies roughly a 10% hike probability, with December near 80%; Rabobank expects Hammack, Kashkari and Logan to repeat their July dissents for a hike. Warsh has rejected traditional forward guidance and his September statement was notably short, so the realistic distribution is a non-committal statement that disappoints a market pricing December at 80%, with the upside case being three hawkish dissents doing the talking instead. DXY is 102.412, a two-week high and its strongest since October 14, up 0.62% on the week. The midterms are six days out with 435 House and 35 Senate seats, and OCBC's own finding is that there is no reliable post-midterm pattern for the dollar - treat it as one more reason the statement does not commit, not as a direction. The euro stays at zero and the balance inside it has shifted. What was repaired yesterday held: the OAT is 4.9220 and its Bund spread about 157 basis points against a 3.3550 Bund, the BTP 4.5100, and Newsquawk's read is that the Moody's affirmation removes enough immediate pressure that a dovish ECB reassessment is unlikely. What got worse is energy, and it got worse fast. EU gas is 96.44 euros per megawatt hour, up 0.65% today but 10.32% on the week, 38.83% on the month and 242.48% year to date; UK gas is 240.10 pence and 11.56% higher on the week. So the split this file traded for a week - crude deflating, gas inflating - has collapsed into both inflating, which is hawkish for every central bank here and a pure cost shock for the euro area and the United Kingdom. Thirty-two of thirty-two houses expect the deposit rate held at 2.50% tomorrow and a Reuters poll has 64 of 73 expecting 25 basis points in December to a 2.75% peak. France will dominate the Q&A, Moody's own baseline assumes the budget eventually passes possibly by decree, and the National Assembly rejected the revenue portion of the social security bill on Friday - so the rating still rests on a government surviving a vote. The franc stays at minus 1 and alone at the bottom on structure, but the tail under the franc shorts got slightly fatter today rather than thinner, and that is worth saying because it cuts against the position. A zero policy rate, a 0.4570% ten-year that is the lowest on this board and 476 basis points below Australia, September CPI of 1.0% with core 0.5%, nothing scheduled until December 10, and an SNB that in its own published September discussion attributed a roughly 3% trade-weighted decline to carry-trade demand, noted little safe-haven interest and judged heightened intervention willingness no longer necessary while keeping the option to act. That is a currency built to be funded in, and IFR reports it displacing the yen as the funding currency of choice as BoJ hikes erode yen funding. The thing that breaks it is exactly what re-escalated today: a Hormuz disruption that persists long enough to turn a supply shock into a demand shock restores the classic haven hierarchy and bids the franc and gold together. UniCredit's warning that a rapid return toward or below March's EUR/CHF low of 0.8981 could prompt direct intervention sits 2.6% below a 0.92294 spot. On the metals, yesterday's calls both worked and neither needs changing. Gold at 4035.52 is down 0.61%, 2.55% on the week, and is doing precisely what RANGE means - holding the 4,000 dealers treat as support while a ten-year back above 5% caps it and a mine strike east of Hormuz bids it, with 18:30 UTC the arbiter. Silver at 53.900 fell another 0.94%, is down 7.00% on the week and 12.29% on the month and sits near an eleven-month low, with copper at 6.6219 and minus 0.08% offering no industrial help; the gold-silver ratio is 74.9. No follow-through plus an unresolved physical read is a RANGE, not a long. So the trade list narrows to the places where the score gap is real and no central bank speaks for weeks. AUD/NZD at 1.25434 is now the cleanest HIGH in the file on a plus 3 against a minus 1, the widest gap on the board, with a verified core beat on one side and a refused hike on the other; it is up 1.42% today, 1.70% on the week and 8.19% year to date. AUD/CHF at 0.58374 keeps its HIGH on a 476 basis point yield spread and no Swiss catalyst until December 10. NZD/USD becomes a MEDIUM short, EUR/NZD and GBP/NZD become MEDIUM longs, and NZD/JPY and NZD/CAD become MEDIUM shorts. NZD/CHF loses its long entirely and goes RANGE, because both legs are now at minus 1 and the score gap is zero - that is the kind of position that quietly stops being a trade. CAD/JPY becomes a LONG on the cleanest divergence here, since the same oil move improves Canada's terms of trade and damages Japan's. Keep sterling exposure small until 12:30 is behind you, keep everything else small until 18:30 is, and note that the only three things on this board without an event inside 48 hours are the franc, the kiwi's next meeting and the Aussie's. Not financial advice.

today.headline: The Reserve Bank held the OCR at 2.75% on a 4-3 vote when a hike to 3.00% was priced between 90% and 100%, and NZD/USD has fallen 1.31% to 0.56073 - lower, not higher, in the hours since a hawkish press conference
today.read: This is the day's largest move and it resolves the question this file left open at 02:00 UTC in the direction that costs the kiwi a point. The surprise was real: four members - Breman, Carl Hansen, Prasanna Gai and Rebecca Williams - held against Conway, Gourley and Silk for 25 basis points, and the currency fell close to a cent in minutes. What matters more is what did not happen afterwards. Breman delivered the hawkish branch explicitly, saying further increases are likely at coming meetings, that policy could move into restrictive territory, that the Committee discussed whether the OCR may need to rise above its projected path, and that it is concerned a sustained weak New Zealand dollar adds to imported inflation. This file read that as a floor, on the argument that a Governor naming the exchange rate as an inflation channel makes further weakness self-limiting. The price then went lower. That leg is broken and the conclusion is straightforward: conditional guidance from a Committee that has just refused a 90%-priced hike carries no premium until the data arrives. Forward, December 9 is genuinely live - a 4-3 vote, a full Monetary Policy Statement, the first new OCR track since September, and a Bank whose own profile has annual CPI rising to 4.4% in the December quarter on fuel futures before returning inside the 1-3% band by mid-2027. But the risks between here and there point down: unemployment at 5.6% and rising, a Q3 CPI that undershot at 3.7%, the ten-year down to 4.9450, and a general election on November 7. The dated triggers Breman named are the partial inflation indicators and the labour market reports of the next six weeks, and the kiwi is a sell into them rather than a hold.

today.headline: The quarterly trimmed mean printed 1.0% q/q against the Reserve Bank's own 0.8% August forecast, confirming what Hauser pre-flagged - and November pricing jumped from 50-60% to between 78% and 90%, with AUD/USD up only 0.12%
today.read: The analytical gap this file flagged yesterday has closed in the hawkish direction, and TradingEconomics carries the number: Trimmed Mean CPI QoQ at 1.0% from 0.8%. That is the Bank's own forecast beaten by two tenths on the measure it targets, on the quarterly frequency where Deputy Governor Hauser said publicly it looked set to beat. With it came the annual trimmed mean at 3.7% against a 3.6% consensus, headline 4.3% y/y against 4.2%, 0.8% m/m against 0.7%, quarterly headline 1.3% q/q and 3.9% y/y, and a weighted median that eased to 3.4% y/y. ANZ says it cements the November case; CBA has switched to a hike. So the data verdict is now the strongest on this board and it is verified rather than inferred. The forward read has to be honest about the other half: the thing this file was buying was an unpriced hawkish decision, and it is no longer unpriced - FXStreet has November at 78% from 70%, Bloomberg data around 85%, the ABC near 90%. AUD/USD responded with plus 0.12% on the day and plus 0.06% on the week, which is the market telling you the repricing is done. What remains is a real rate differential about to widen further from the highest policy rate here, and the right place to own it is against currencies with no catalyst or a broken one - the franc at 476 basis points below with nothing until December 10, and the kiwi after a refused hike. The live risk into November 3 is the labour market: another soft employment report after minus 39,329, with a 47.8 services PMI and business confidence at minus 13, hands the hold camp the argument that the Bank is tightening into a contraction.

today.headline: WTI back at 101.423 and up 4.40% on the week restores the terms-of-trade leg, and Macklem's Saturday remark that quarterly inflation forecasts will likely be revised higher moved futures from about 30% to roughly three in four for today's hike
today.read: Both reasons this file cut Canada yesterday are now half-repaired, eight and a half hours before the decision. The commodity leg is the cleaner of the two: the barrel is up 1.52% today and 4.40% on the week on a re-escalating Hormuz story, which is a direct terms-of-trade gain for the one G10 economy here that exports crude, with the caveat that a 14.08 dollar Brent-WTI spread means Canadian grades capture less of the move than Brent headlines suggest. The policy leg is the Governor himself, which is a stronger signal than any house view: Macklem told reporters on Saturday that the Bank's quarterly inflation forecasts are likely to be revised higher, and a forty-point jump in futures pricing is the market agreeing. What has not closed is the forecaster split, and that is why Canada stays at plus 1 rather than going to plus 2 in front of a binary: a Reuters poll of 34 economists has 56% expecting 25 basis points to 2.50% against pricing near 75-80%, and TD has argued the Bank can stay on hold this year on softer employment, a weak housing market and tariff risk. The supporting hawkish evidence is unchanged - five-year inflation expectations at 3.91% from 3.39% in the Q3 Business Outlook Survey, 16 of 29 economists expecting a second increase to 2.75% by end-March - and September CPI at 3.1% against 2.2% excluding gasoline is itself the energy channel Macklem said gets harder to look through. Forward, the Monetary Policy Report's inflation profile outlives the decision, and a hold would be the sharper move because it is the less-priced one.

today.headline: The yen lost the energy tailwind this file was leaning on - crude stopped deflating, USD/JPY has held near 158 at 157.807, and with the US ten-year back above 5% at 5.0250 the yield disadvantage widened to about 219 basis points
today.read: This is a mark-down on a named leg rather than on the policy case, and it is worth separating the two. Yesterday's read said in terms that a deflating crude premium gives something to the yen as the most energy-import-levered economy on this board. Crude did not keep deflating, and the transmission showed up immediately: the yen could not hold its gains through the Asian session and reporting attributes that directly to higher import costs, while the JGB rose to 2.8310 but the US ten-year rose further to 5.0250, so the spread moved against it. The policy case is intact and still the most improved on this board over the past month - 83% of economists now expect a December hike against 35% a month ago, MUFG expects Friday's Outlook Report to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached 2%, Reuters frames it as the Bank declaring victory in a nearly fourteen-year battle, and Daiwa expects FY26 growth lifted to 0.8% and FY27 core CPI to 2.5%. USD.when: Today, October 28, at 18:00 UTC with Chair Warsh's press conference at 18:30. A Reuters poll has 94 of 100 economists expecting no change and CME FedWatch implies roughly a 10% hike probability; December 8-9 is the live meeting at about 80%.
USD.note: TradingEconomics re-verified the fed funds target range at 3.75-4.00%, upper bound 4.00%, after the unanimous September 16 hike. The decision is not the event and the statement barely is: Warsh has rejected traditional forward guidance, his September statement was notably short, and with December already near 80% there is almost nothing hawkish left for him to deliver and considerable room to disappoint. The hawkish route runs through the dissents rather than the Chair - Rabobank expects Hammack, Kashkari and Logan to repeat their July votes for a hike, which would offset a non-committal statement. Today's data backdrop turned mildly hawkish on its own: the ten-year is back above 5% at 5.0250 and WTI is up 4.40% on the week, against September CPI at 3.7%, core 2.6%, core PCE 3.0% and only 29,000 jobs added. No projections or dot plot today - those come on December 9. The midterms are six days out with 435 House and 35 Senate seats; OCBC finds no reliable post-midterm pattern for the dollar, so read it as another reason the statement does not commit.

EUR.when: Tomorrow, October 29, at 13:15 UTC with Lagarde at 13:45. Research tracked by FinChiefs has 32 of 32 houses expecting a hold, and a Reuters poll has 64 of 73 expecting 25 basis points in December to a 2.75% peak deposit rate.
EUR.note: TradingEconomics carries the deposit facility rate at 2.50% and the main refinancing rate at 2.65% after the September 10 hike; ForexFactory's red folder is the refi line at an unchanged 2.65%. Moody's own baseline assumes the budget eventually passes, possibly by decree, and the National Assembly rejected the revenue portion of the social security bill on Friday, so the rating rests on a government surviving a vote. GBP.when: November 5 at 12:00 UTC, priced at 94-97% for 25 basis points to 4.00%. The Annual Budget lands eight days earlier at 12:30 UTC today and reshapes the fiscal backdrop the Committee forecasts against.
GBP.note: TradingEconomics re-verified Bank Rate at 3.75%. TradingEconomics describes gilt markets as unusually calm going in despite ambitious spending plans not yet fully costed, and an FP Markets preview makes the pound's reaction conditional on why yields move - a growth-driven rise is sterling-positive, a risk-driven rise sterling-negative. JPY.when: October 30 at 02:30 UTC with the Outlook Report at 02:31 and Ueda at 05:30. A Bloomberg survey has 83% of economists expecting a December hike, up from 35% a month ago, with none expecting a move on Friday; the December meeting ends December 18.
JPY.note: TradingEconomics re-verified the policy rate at 1.25% after the September 18 hike. The new input since yesterday is energy, and it cuts the other way from the policy case: crude up 4.40% on the week is a direct terms-of-trade hit to the most energy-import-levered economy here. CHF.when: December 10 - still the only scheduled Swiss event on the horizon, and six weeks away while four other central banks speak inside three days. Most analysts see no increase before 2028.

catalysts.note: Released. The market's answer is the information: NZD/USD went lower rather than higher in the hours after, which withdraws the floor argument this file made at 02:00 UTC. catalysts.note: Chancellor John Healey's first Budget, and the nearest risk in this file. TradingEconomics describes gilt markets as unusually calm going in despite ambitious spending plans that have not been fully costed, which is the configuration where the asymmetry sits on the downside. Headroom estimates have clustered near 15 billion pounds in a 12-18 billion range against the 23.6 billion the OBR forecast in March, the bank surcharge is expected to rise from 3% to 8%, and Newsquawk has had the gilt remit up by as much as 10 billion. An FP Markets preview makes the pound's reaction conditional on why yields move: a growth-driven rise is sterling-positive, a risk-driven rise sterling-negative. The ten-year gilt at 5.3529 is the highest yield on this board.

The Monetary Policy Report's inflation profile outlives the decision, and 16 of 29 economists already expect a second increase to 2.75% by end-March. WTI back at 101.423 restores the terms-of-trade leg.

Macklem has already warned that persistent energy prices get harder to look through, and September CPI at 3.1% against 2.2% excluding gasoline is that channel in the data. The Q3 Business Outlook Survey's five-year inflation expectations at 3.91% from 3.39% is the strongest piece of hawkish evidence he has. Listen for whether a hike is framed as the first of a sequence or as insurance against the energy pass-through.

catalysts.note: The single biggest asymmetry in this file. Warsh has rejected traditional forward guidance and his September statement was notably short, so with December already 80% priced there is almost nothing hawkish left for him to deliver and considerable room to disappoint. The structural read is that a non-committal Chair sells the dollar; the counter-case is that three regional dissents do the hawkish work for him. The midterms are six days out with 435 House and 35 Senate seats, and one analysis argues he may feel pressure not to pre-commit with the vote that close; OCBC finds no reliable post-midterm pattern for the dollar.

catalysts.event: Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf energy infrastructure
catalysts.note: Re-escalated on October 27, when Iran's navy said a tanker caught fire after striking naval mines east of the strait and that the strait remains unsafe and closed to vessels crossing without coordination - unverified independently, as with the October 17 claim. Reuters counts at least eighteen tanker attacks in two weeks on Kpler data and the US is urging shippers onto a southern route Tehran calls illegal. Against that, Iran's ambassador says Tehran remains open to an interim deal brokered with Pakistan and Qatar, and Araghchi's seven-day plan would reopen the strait if the US lifts its port blockade.

geopolitics: The transmission chain this file trades - Iran and the Strait of Hormuz into oil, oil into headline inflation, headline inflation into central banks that cannot ease - re-engaged today at the oil end after three sessions of running in reverse, and it did so on a dated incident rather than on sentiment. Iran's navy said on Tuesday October 27 that an oil tanker caught fire after striking naval mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, that the vessel had switched off its tracking and entered a restricted zone, and that the strait remains unsafe and closed to ships attempting to pass without coordination. There is no independent confirmation of that account, exactly as there was none for the October 17 claim, and that is worth stating because the market is pricing the claim and not a verified event. Reuters, on Kpler data, counts at least eighteen tanker attacks over the last two weeks, and the United States is urging shippers onto a southern route through the strait that Tehran regards as illegal - which is the part of the story that makes an accident or a deliberate strike more likely rather than less. WTI is 101.423 and up 1.52%, 4.40% on the week, 13.47% on the month and 76.63% year to date; Brent is 115.502 and up 1.42% and 6.14% on the week, with the Brent-WTI spread widening to 14.08 dollars, which remains the disruption signature - the residual premium accrues to seaborne crude rather than to the landlocked US benchmark, which is why Canadian grades capture less of any oil move than Brent headlines imply. Now the part this file has to correct about its own reasoning, because the error was in the inference rather than in the evidence. For two days this file built the case that the premium was deflating because the barrels were rerouting, and that evidence is intact and was never in doubt: strait flows are back near 82% of pre-war levels, total Middle East oil flows averaged more than 24 million barrels a day last week against 23.3 million before the war on Kpler data, 40% of non-Iranian Gulf crude now moves by pipeline against 17% pre-war, and US military escorts are shuttling tankers in the Gulf of Oman. What was wrong was the conclusion drawn from it. A risk premium is not priced off volumes delivered, it is priced off insurable risk, and a mine field reprices insurance regardless of how many barrels get through. Rerouting caps the upside on the premium; it does not deflate it while the mines are still being laid. That is why USOIL goes long today after a week at range, and why the loonie gets its terms-of-trade leg back nine hours before its central bank decides. The diplomatic channel is live and unchanged, and it is the live invalidation on the long. Iran's ambassador says Tehran remains open to talks under an interim deal brokered with Pakistan and Qatar and has used Pakistan to offer reopening the strait if Washington lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports; Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran is still reviewing US comments on its seven-day plan and that its conditions stand - the strait reopens on day six and negotiations begin on day seven if the United States lifts the blockade and eases sanctions. Trump rejected that proposal when it was first floated in September but says the US is still talking, and diplomatic contacts continue among Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Iran. Earlier US-Iran talks broke down over navigation rules for the strait, which is precisely the question the southern-route dispute turns on. So the channel is contested rather than closed, and a single headline from it unwinds today's oil move faster than the mines put it on. The gas channel did not pause and on the week it accelerated again, and the significant change today is that the split this file has been trading for a week has collapsed. EU gas is 96.44 euros per megawatt hour, up 0.65% today but 10.32% on the week, 38.83% on the month and 242.48% year to date; UK gas is 240.10 pence per therm and 11.56% higher on the week and 225.29% on the year; German gas is 95.89 euros and 219.61% higher on the year. Put the two series side by side on a weekly basis: crude up 4.40% and EU gas up 10.32%. Yesterday the crude premium was deflating while the gas premium inflated, and the whole shape of the board followed from that asymmetry - it took the commodity leg from the loonie, gave something to the yen and left the euro area untouched. Today both are inflating, and the consequences invert accordingly. The loonie gets its leg back. The yen loses the one input this file was crediting it with and comes down a point, because Japan is the most energy-import-levered economy here and a crude shock lands on it directly. The euro area and the United Kingdom are now taking both shocks at once, which is hawkish for the ECB and the Bank of England in a way neither can enjoy, because it is a cost shock with no export offset. And every central bank on this board now has a harder inflation argument to make than it did twenty-four hours ago - which is exactly the backdrop against which Warsh has to decline to give guidance at 18:30 UTC. On the regime, be explicit that yesterday's call lasted one session and say why that matters. Yesterday every ten-year here fell while equities rose, and this file read it as an inflation premium coming out rather than a growth scare. Today the US ten-year is back above 5% at 5.0250, the JGB rose to 2.8310, the Australian ten-year to 5.2200, the OAT to 4.9220 and the BTP to 4.5100, with only New Zealand on its own dovish surprise and a 0.4570% Switzerland lower. Equities kept their bid - the S&P near 7,723 and up 0.60%, the Nasdaq Composite 26,478 and up 1.18%, the Nikkei 63,268 and up 1.73%, the DAX 25,541.50 and up 0.71%, the VIX down to 17.52 - so the configuration is equities up with yields up, which is an inflation premium going back in. The honest lesson is that one session of falling yields inside an energy shock is a rally, not a regime change, and this file should not have labelled it one. Gold is still the asset refusing to confirm either story: at 4035.52 and down 0.61% it is holding the 4,000 dealers treat as support, capped by a ten-year above 5% and bid by the mines, which is why it stays at range with 18:30 UTC as the arbiter. The franc remains the funding currency and the SNB has explained why in its own words - a roughly 3% trade-weighted decline since June attributed to carry demand, little safe-haven interest, heightened intervention willingness judged no longer necessary - but today's escalation moved the tail against every franc short rather than for it, and that deserves saying out loud rather than burying. So the structure of the trade is unchanged and its composition has shifted. Own the currency whose central bank still has a decision the market has not fully bought - and after today that is a shorter list, because Australia's November hike went from 50-60% to near 90% and New Zealand's did not happen at all. Fund it in the currency that cannot respond for six weeks. The two invalidations point opposite ways and both are now sharper. The first is diplomatic: an interim deal through Pakistan and Qatar unwinds the crude premium, takes the oil-linked hawkish pricing with it and reverses today's loonie improvement and today's oil long. The second is the one that breaks every franc short here and it got closer rather than further today - a disruption that persists long enough to convert a supply shock into a demand shock would restore the classic haven hierarchy, bid the franc and gold together and invert most of these crosses. The tells are specific: gold losing 4,000, a rise in the Navy-led JMIC threat level, and a tanker loss large enough to stop the convoys. Watch the Kpler and Vortexa volume series for the physical picture, but price the premium off the security picture, because this week demonstrated that those two can move in opposite directions on the same day.
